newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Washington sees light in darkest Africa.
newsitem.headline: Washington sees light in darkest Africa.

text.p: Africa is back on Washington's radar screen, the latest sign that things are starting to go right on the world's poorest continent.

The sudden U.S. interest in Africa, evidenced by President Bill Clinton's economic plan for the continent this week, reflects a growing confidence that democracy and economic reform are taking root, analysts said on Wednesday.

For the U.S., often accused of neglecting Africa in the past, the time appears right to promote investment in a continent which remains a giant storehouse of mineral and oil wealth, as well as a large potential market.

After the lost decade of the 1980s, Africa is getting its house in order with 37 of the 48 sub-Saharan states undertaking serious economic reform, including tariff reduction, privatisation and easing investment laws, according to the World Bank.
They may not be Asian Tigers, but a growing number of African lion cubs are starting to test their roars.

In the continent as a whole, economies achieved growth of around five percent last year and are on course for a similar performance this year, while a few stars like Uganda, Mozambique and Ethiopia are well into double digits.

They now stand to gain from the programme of tariff cuts, investment promotion and faster debt relief which the U.S. has pledged to lobby for at this week's summit of leading industrial nations in Denver.
"A lot of low-tech value-added industries in sub-Saharan Africa could be big winners if they get access to the U.S. market," said Tony Twine of Econometrix consultancy in Johannesburg.
He sees the U.S. initiative -- which could also help the U.S. cut its trade imbalance with Asia by shopping elsewhere -- as a vital prop to the often brittle democracies of the sub-Saharan region.
"There is one way to give democracy an extra chance and that is to ensure that it thrives economically," Twine said.

Under the Clinton plan, an additional 1,800 products from the poorest countries in Africa would receive duty-free access to the U.S. while nations undertaking concerted economic reform would benefit from reduced tariffs.

"If that means removal of quotas, say on items such as shirts Kenya exports to the U.S., that is really practical and will encourage higher production from Africa," Kenya's central bank governor Micah Cheserem told Reuters.
"If the G7 countries follow up by saying that they will open trade to Africa, then that would be a major step forward."
But the key to shifting Africa's economies up a gear lies in boosting private sector investment.
On the global stage, Africa remains largely a lost continent, attracting a mere three percent of the foreign direct investment that is going into developing countries.

Clinton's plans for a $150 million equity fund to increase private investment and a $500 million fund for infrastructure investment will help and, crucially, could swing sentiment among wary U.S. investors.

"The initiative represents opening up of Africa to new opportunities, it is reminding American investors that Africa does exist," said Joseph Kimura, senior economist at the private Institute of Policy Analysis and Research in Nairobi.
Tony Hawkins, Professor of Business Studies at The University of Zimbabwe, is more sceptical.
"You can lead the horse to water but getting the American investor to drink will be much more difficult when there are so many competing investment locations around the world," he said.
Hawkins is also dubious about the impact of U.S. tariff relief on Africa's export industry.
"Sadly, all the work that has been done on African exports shows it is not tariff barriers that are the problem, but other things, such as transport problems and quality," he said.
Debt relief is another area of concern to African observers.
Clinton's words are fine, but what will it mean in terms of trimming Africa's international debt, which totals some $340 billion and chews up $24 billion annually in servicing costs?

Cheick Fall, secretary-general of the African Development Bank in Abidjan, said Clinton's comments on debt relief suggested a move beyond the Highly Indebted Poor Countries (HIPC) scheme already operated by the International Monetary Fund and World Bank.
But he regretted the lack of detail.
"You will notice that in all the items except debt they (the Americans) were quite clear...On debt they only said 'help' for African countries."
